The Five Classical Orders of Architecture. The standardized systems of proportion, style, and ornamentation used in ancient Greek and Roman buildings have been codified by Renaissance and Baroque theorists. Three orders—Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian—originated in classical Greece, and two later composite orders—Tuscan and Composite—were developed by Romans. These orders have dominated Western architecture for over two millennia, providing a shared visual language for columns, capitals, and overall structure.

The Doric order is the simplest and most austere, featuring fluted columns with no base, plain echinus capitals, and a sturdy male-coded aesthetic, employed in Greek temples and Roman civic structures. The Ionic order is more slender and graceful than Doric, with a base, an elaborate capital crowned by scrolls called volutes, and fluted shafts, associated with female elegance in classical aesthetics. The Corinthian order is the most ornate and luxurious, with an ornamental capital decorated with acanthus leaves, used extensively in Roman temples and later aristocratic buildings. The Tuscan order is a Roman simplification of the Doric, with unfluted columns, a base, and minimal ornament, practical and economical for utilitarian Roman structures. The Composite order is a Roman synthesis combining the Ionic scrolls with the Corinthian acanthus leaves, used in triumphal arches and grand imperial buildings.

The orders are defined by strict mathematical proportions of height-to-width ratios, capital height, and entablature composition, systematized in treatises by Vitruvius, Palladio, and later theorists.
